newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CSFB raises earnings, target for Roche.
newsitem.headline: CSFB raises earnings, target for Roche.

text.p: Investment bank Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB) is raising its earnings estimates and price target for Roche Holding AG following the company's annual research and development presentation on Monday.
Earnings estimates were raised on the basis of an increase in sales estimates of three new drugs, CSFB's head of pharma research Genghis Lloyd-Harris wrote in a research note.
He added that Roche's 11 percent increase in 1996 group sales had exceed his expectation by 2.1 percent.
CSFB raised its price target for Roche's non-voting equity securities (NES) to 14,000 Swiss francs going into 1998, up from a previous target of 13,600 francs.
The target represents a 14 percent premium to yesterday's closing price of 12,285 francs.
The 1996 earnings per share (EPS) estimate has been raised to 465 francs from a previous 457, the 1997 estimate to 544 from 532 and the 1998 estimate to 620 from 607 francs
This compares with a 1995 EPS of 391 francs.
CSFB's increased its sales forecast for three drugs -- CellCept, Xenical and Posicor -- and the estimates now match Roche's own estimates.

Annual sales for CellCept, an immunosuppressant for renal transplants, was raised to 600 million francs or more from a previous estimate of 500 million francs. CSFB's estimate now matches Roche's own estimate.
Annual sales for Xenical, a treatment for obesity, are now estimated at 700 million francs or more, up from a previous estimate of 550 million. This also matches Roche's estimate.
Annual sales for Posicor, a calcium channel blocker, are estimated at 800 million francs, up from a previous estimate of 700 million.

In addition to the presentation of drugs, Roche also revealed its new strategy for developing drugs that aims at cutting costs by 40 percent, partially from process improvement and partially by early elimination of unsuccessful drugs.
CSFB also noted that Roche had set up an experiment to accelerate drug development, which they refer to as a "virtual company."

Just as it has long been recognised that small biotech companies have advantages in drug discovery, Roche is exploring the idea that a small group of experienced individuals may be able to develop drugs faster than a larger "machine."
Individuals participating in this experiment are paid high salaries and so far three compounds, one late stage and two early stage, have been put into the virtual company, CSFB said.
